the study of radiation-induced damage in macromolecular crystals and with the development of strategies to reduce this damage.

the development of methods for reducing radiation damage in biological macromolecular crystallography and for improving the quality of the resulting diffraction data, which are essential prerequisites for the structural determination of macromolecular complexes.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the quick soaking approach is an easy and effective way to protect crystals and increase their lifetime in the X-Ray beam.
the quick soaking method is a very effective tool for reducing radiation damage to crystals and that it should be considered in all cases where radiation damage is a problem.
the quick-soaking approach is a valuable tool for crystallographers, which, if properly applied, can be expected to increase the quality of the diffraction data and hence of the structure solution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the quick-soak procedure can increase crystal lifetime by up to 200% for a variety of crystal types.

the use of scavengers is an effective way to increase the lifetime of a crystal, and thus the number of data frames collected, which in turn can increase the quality of the diffraction data and hence the quality of the structure.
we have developed a simple method to extend the lifetime of macromolecular crystals in the X-ray beams and to increase the quality of the diffraction data.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the use of scavengers is a simple yet powerful tool that can be employed to extend the lifetime of a crystal in the X-ray radiation field.
it is possible to protect crystals by soaking them with scavenging compounds, and that this protection can be achieved by soaking the crystals with scavengers for as little as 30 s.

the quick soak procedure is a very simple, inexpensive and fast method that allows the user to obtain diffraction data of higher resolution and quality from a single crystal, and hence to increase significantly the information content of the experiment.
